title: General and special linear groups
section: Part B: Abstract Algebra ▷ Examples of Groups
terms: general linear group; special linear group; matrix group; GL(n,F); SL(n,F); unimodular matrix.

exposition.text:
For a field F, GL(n, F ) is the group of invertible n × n matrices under multiplication. Its sub-
group SL(n, F ) consists of determinant-one matrices. The determinant is multiplicative, so
determinant restrictions often identify subgroups; a restriction such as determinant 2 does not.
Standard notation GL(n, Z) means matrices invertible over Z, equivalently integer matrices of
determinant ±1. All nonsingular integer matrices form only a monoid. Over F , choose inde-

An integer matrix of determinant ±1 is called unimodular here; its integer inverse shows that it
preserves the greatest common divisor of vector coordinates. In particular it preserves primitive
integer vectors, whose coordinate gcd is one. Positive determinant matrices form a subgroup
over R, whereas a fixed determinant other than one need not define a subgroup.

question.text:
How many elements does SL(2, F ) contain?
3
(A) 12 (B) 18 (C) 24 (D) 36 (E) 48

solution.text:
2
The first column of an invertible matrix has 3 − 1 = 8 choices; the second avoids its
three-element span, giving 6 choices. Thus GL has 48 elements. Determinants 1 and 2
occur equally often, so SL has 24.

For how many integers k is invertible over Z?
k 2
(A) 0 (B) 1 (C) 2 (D) 3 (E) Infinitely many

solution.text:
An integer matrix has an integer inverse exactly when its determinant is ±1. Here 4 − 3k = 1
gives k = 1, whereas 4 − 3k = −1 gives the noninteger 5/3. Exactly one integer works.

Positive determinants contain the identity and stay positive under products and reciprocals,
so the subgroup test holds. Each other set omits the identity: its determinant is one, its
trace is two, and its off-diagonal entries are zero.

Let A ∈ GL(2, Z) and let v ∈ Z have relatively prime coordinates. Which must hold for Av?
(A) Its coordinates are positive.
(B) Its Euclidean norm equals that of v.
(C) Its coordinates are relatively prime.
(D) At least one coordinate equals one.
(E) It equals v or −v.

solution.text:
−1
Both A and A have integer entries. Every common divisor of the coordinates of Av
−1
divides those of A (Av) = v, so that divisor is one. More generally the coordinate gcd
is preserved in both directions. Such matrices preserve primitive integer vectors, not
necessarily their lengths.

question.text:
2
If A ∈ SL(2, R) and A = I, which conclusion is forced?
(A) A = I (B) A = −I (C) A = I or A = −I (D) tr A = 0 (E) A is singular

solution.text:
2 2
Cayley–Hamilton gives A − (tr A)A + I = 0. Using A = I yields (tr A)A = 2I, so the
trace is nonzero and A is scalar. Its square being I then forces the scalar to be 1 or −1.
The determinant-one restriction excludes the nontrivial planar reflections.
